chunks: ʿAlī narrated from his father, from Muḥammad ibn al-Walīd, from Muḥammad ibn al-Furāt, from al-Aṣbagh ibn Nubātah, who said:

Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام was asked about a man who struck another man on his head, and the one struck claimed that he could not see anything, that he could not smell scent, and that his tongue had gone.
So Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام said: “If he is truthful, then he is entitled to three blood-compensations.” It was said: O Amīr al-Muʾminīn, then how can it be known that he is truthful?

He said: “As for his claim that he cannot smell any odor, a burning object is brought near him; if he is as he says, otherwise he will move his head away and his eye will tear. As for what he claimed regarding his eye, his eye is faced toward the sun; if he is lying, he will not be able to restrain himself from closing his eye, but if he is truthful, they will remain open. And as for what he claimed regarding his tongue, his tongue is pricked with a needle; if the blood comes out red, then he has lied, and if it comes out black, then he has spoken the truth.”

key_terms.الرَّائِحَةَ: odor or scent, referring here to the sense of smell
key_terms.الْإِبْرَةِ: the needle used to test the tongue
key_terms.الْحُرَّاقُ: a burning object brought near to test the sense of smell
key_terms.عَيْنِهِ: his eye, referring here to the claimed loss of sight
key_terms.لِسَانُهُ: his tongue, referring here to the claimed loss of speech
key_terms.هَامَتِهِ: the top of his head or skull

ai.seo_question: How did Amīr al-Muʾminīn ʿAlī عليه السلام rule on compensation for injuries causing loss of sight, smell, and speech?
ai.summary: This hadith records a legal ruling from Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام concerning bodily injury that allegedly caused loss of sight, smell, and speech. If the claim is true, three separate diyahs are due, and practical methods are given for testing the truthfulness of the injured person’s claims in a judicial context.
